heath_proof: For let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the fourth binomial AD divided into its terms at E, of which terms let AE be the greater; I say that the “side” of the area AC is the irrational straight line called major. For, since AD is a fourth binomial straight line, therefore AE, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE, and AE is commensurable in length with AB. [X. Deff. II. 4] Let DE be bisected at F, and let there be applied to AE a parallelogram, the rectangle AG, GE, equal to the square on EF; therefore AG is incommensurable in length with GE. [X. 18] Let GH, EK, FL be drawn parallel to AB, and let the rest of the construction be as before; it is then manifest that MO is the “side” of the area AC. It is next to be proved that MO is the irrational straight line called major. Since AG is incommensurable with EG, AH is also incommensurable with GK, that is, SN with NQ; [VI. 1, X. 11] therefore MN, NO are incommensurable in square. And, since AE is commensurable with AB, AK is rational; [X. 19] and it is equal to the squares on MN, NO; therefore the sum of the squares on MN, NO is also rational. And, since DE is incommensurable in length with AB, that is, with EK, while DE is commensurable with EF, therefore EF is incommensurable in length with EK. [X. 13] Therefore EK, EF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore LE, that is, MR, is medial. [X. 21] And it is contained by MN, NO; therefore the rectangle MN, NO is medial. And the [sum]of the squares on MN, NO is rational, and MN, NO are incommensurable in square. But, if two straight lines incommensurable in square and making the sum of the squares on them rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial, be added together, the whole is irrational and is called major. [X. 39] Therefore MO is the irrational straight line called major and is the “side” of the area AC.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called major.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the fourth binomial straight line AD. Let AD be divided into its terms at E, with AE the greater term and ED the lesser. We must show that the "side" of the area AC is the irrational straight line called major.

**Step 2.** By the definition of a fourth binomial (D10.2.4), AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE; and AE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB.

**Step 3.** Since AE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB, the rectangle AB times AE is rational, by 10.19.

**Step 4.** Since AE and ED are commensurable in square only (from the binomial, by 10.36), ED is incommensurable in length with AE. Since AE is commensurable in length with AB, by 10.13 ED is incommensurable in length with AB. Therefore the rectangle AB times ED is medial, by 10.21.

**Step 5.** Bisect ED at the point F, so that EF equals half of ED, by 1.10. Then the square on ED equals four times the square on EF. Apply to AE a rectangle equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure, by 6.28: find a point G on AE such that AG times GE equals the square on EF. Thus four times AG times GE equals the square on ED.

**Step 6.** Since the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE (D10.2.4), and the rectangle AG times GE equals one-fourth of the square on ED, by 10.18 AG is incommensurable in length with GE.

**Step 7.** Set r and s to be straight lines such that the square on r equals the rectangle AB times AG, and the square on s equals the rectangle AB times GE.

**Step 8.** Then the sum of the squares on r and s equals AB times AG plus AB times GE, which equals AB times (AG + GE), which equals AB times AE (since G lies on AE so that AG + GE = AE). By Step 3, AB times AE is rational. Therefore the sum of the squares on r and s is rational.

**Step 9.** By 6.17, the square on r times the square on s equals (AB times AG) times (AB times GE) equals the square on AB times the rectangle AG times GE. Since AG times GE equals the square on EF (Step 5), this equals the square on AB times the square on EF, which equals the square on (AB times EF). Therefore r times s equals AB times EF. Since EF equals half of ED, we have 2 times r times s equals AB times ED, which is medial by Step 4.

**Step 10.** Since AG is incommensurable in length with GE (Step 6), by 6.1 and 10.11 the rectangle AB times AG is incommensurable with the rectangle AB times GE (AB being a common side). That is, the square on r is incommensurable with the square on s. Therefore r and s are incommensurable in square.

**Step 11.** We verify that 2rs is incommensurable with r squared plus s squared. The square on (r times s) equals the square on AB times the square on EF (Step 9). The square on (r squared plus s squared) equals the square on (AB times AE), which equals the square on AB times the square on AE. The ratio of the square on (r times s) to the square on (r squared plus s squared) equals the square on EF to the square on AE, which equals the square on ED to four times the square on AE (since EF equals half of ED). Since AE and ED are rational and commensurable in square only, the square on AE is incommensurable with the square on ED. Therefore the square on (r times s) is incommensurable with the square on (r squared plus s squared), and hence 2rs is incommensurable with r squared plus s squared, by 6.1 and 10.11.

**Step 12.** Now let w equal r plus s. Then the square on w equals the square on r plus the square on s plus twice the rectangle r times s, by 2.4. This equals AB times AE plus AB times ED, which equals AB times (AE + ED), which equals AB times AD, which is the area AC.

**Step 13.** We have established that r and s are two straight lines such that: (i) they are incommensurable in square (Step 10); (ii) the sum of the squares on them is rational (Step 8); and (iii) twice the rectangle contained by them is medial (Step 9). Therefore, by 10.39, the straight line w equals r plus s is the irrational line called major.

**Step 14.** Since the square on w equals the area AC (Step 12), the "side" of the area AC is the major irrational straight line. This is what was to be proved.
